tagline: Ore-wagon roads over two 12,000-foot passes, and seven ghost towns.
intro: The loop usually starts in Lake City and heads west into the San Juan Mountains, over Cinnamon Pass or Engineer Pass to Animas Forks, then comes back east over the other. The loop also reaches Silverton and Ouray. Ouray sits at a mere 7,792 feet. Engineer Pass tops out at 12,800. The pavement stays behind.

These are the roads 19th-century miners used to haul ore to Silverton, Ouray and Lake City in mule-drawn wagons, and seven ghost towns are left along them. Drivers who go clockwise, Cinnamon first, keep the inside lane on the mountain stretches, with the driver on the outside where the edge of the drop-off is easier to judge.

moments.title: Henson
moments.text: A ghost town at 9,236 feet, spelled Hansen, Hanson, Hensen and Honsen until the Board on Geographic Names settled the matter in 1896.

moments.title: Capitol City
moments.text: Founded as Galena City in 1877 and renamed in hope of becoming the state capital, it keeps a post office, a smelter stack and a few brick kilns.

moments.title: Animas Forks
moments.text: One of the highest mining camps in North America, at 11,185 feet, where a 23-day blizzard in 1884 left 25 feet of snow and people tunneled between buildings.

practical: Cinnamon and Engineer passes require a high-clearance four-wheel-drive vehicle, and the loop is closed in winter.
